title: Why Your AR Backlog Is an Infrastructure Problem—Not a Staffing Problem
summary: A growing AR backlog is often a sign of weak data, limited IT capacity, manual work, and unclear ownership—not simply a shortage of staff.
body_markdown:
*Why more people cannot compensate for weak data, limited IT capacity, manual work, and unclear ownership*


**By Vanessa Couch-Laguana, Head of RCM, LunaBill**


---


Hiring more people into a weak workflow can simply scale the inefficiency.


## The backlog is usually telling us something


When an AR backlog grows, the first response is often to add staff, outsource accounts, or increase productivity expectations. Those actions may create temporary capacity, but they do not necessarily address why the backlog formed. In my experience, the underlying problem is usually more complicated than a shortage of people.


Revenue Cycle leaders are expected to size productivity and correct performance while working with limited IT support, incomplete analysis, and systems that may not be configured to support the workflow. At the same time, competing priorities continue to arrive. By the time one problem is understood, a new project takes precedence. The backlog keeps accumulating because neither operations nor IT has enough protected capacity to redesign the work.


## Leaders need to know what should be automated


A sustainable operating model begins by separating predictable transactional work from work that requires specialized judgment. Basic code mapping, timely claim-status responses, routing from electronic responses, eligibility verification, and other repeatable actions should not depend on a person noticing every issue.


The same principle applies upstream. At scheduling, organizations should capture accurate insurance information, verify eligibility, estimate patient responsibility, and begin appropriate pre-collection efforts. Orders and procedures should route to the right authorization workflow. Charges and notes should be completed promptly. Edits should be resolved before a clean claim leaves the organization.


Every defect that could have been prevented on the front end becomes more expensive rework on the back end. A billing office should not have to reconstruct information that was available at the first patient contact.


## Specialized work still belongs with specialized people


Automation does not eliminate the need for experienced Revenue Cycle professionals. Contract interpretation, payment-variance review, medical-necessity disputes, clinical evidence, and persuasive appeals require judgment. A system may flag the variance or assemble relevant information, but the decision and argument may still need a human touch.


This is also true when care changes. Extended stays, added procedures, or movement between behavioral and medical settings should trigger timely clinical review. Those issues belong with utilization management, care management, case management, or another qualified clinical operation—not with a biller trying to justify medical necessity after discharge.


## Infrastructure means data, workflow, ownership, and time


The word infrastructure is sometimes interpreted as technology alone. It is broader than that. Infrastructure includes timely analysis, clear decision rights, sufficient IT support, appropriately configured work queues, service-level expectations, escalation paths, and leaders who have time to act on what the data reveals.


Hiring more people into a weak workflow can simply scale the inefficiency. The more durable answer is to prevent avoidable defects, automate predictable volume, route specialized work correctly, and make the next action visible. When those elements are in place, staffing discussions become much more grounded because leaders can see the work that genuinely requires human capacity.
